$note: The protection this repository's branches are supposed to have. GitHub does not read this file —
nothing can, because branch protection is settings rather than content. What it does is make the
intent reviewable: `node .github/scripts/branch-protection.mjs` prints the drift between this and
reality and exits 1, `--apply` writes this file to GitHub, and `--selftest` checks the comparison
logic without a token. Every branch named under `branches` is checked, and the exit code is the
worst of them — 0 all match, 1 one drifts, 3 one could not be looked at.
$decided: TWO branches, with DIFFERENT protection, because they are moved in different ways. `main` is where
rules are WRITTEN and it is pull-request-only. `release` is what six consumers LOAD, and it is moved
by promote-release.yml pushing <sha>:refs/heads/release directly — so requiring a pull request there
would break the only supported way to move it. See .github/workflows/promote-release.yml, which has
recorded this ref's exposure as an accepted risk since 2026-09-14.
The contexts are the check names GitHub ACTUALLY reported on recent merged pull requests, not
names read out of the workflows: a required check that never reports blocks every pull request
forever. Deliberately NOT here: `ask CodeRabbit` (a third-party free tier that runs out —
requiring it puts every merge behind somebody else’s quota), `github-advanced-security` and the
`Analyze (…)` legs (umbrella and per-language parts of CodeQL, which is required), and
`SonarCloud Code Analysis` (Sonar’s own gate, distinct from the `SonarCloud Scan` job — making
the gate blocking is its own decision).
WHAT THIS CLOSES: `release` can no longer be rewound, deleted, or given a non-linear history,
and an admin is not exempt. Those are the failures that would hurt every consumer at once —
promote-release.yml says so itself: moving the ref backwards makes all six repositories' pinned
shas differ from the tip during the very incident a rollback exists to end.
AND THE CHECKS ARE REQUIRED AFTER ALL. The first version of this file said they would merely
duplicate promote-release.mjs, and that was wrong in a way worth recording: `forward` constrains
ANCESTRY, not CONTENT. A single-parent child of the current release tip carrying anything at all
is a forward move, and it need never have been on main. Required checks apply to a DIRECT PUSH,
not only to a merge, so a hand-pushed commit that never ran ci is now refused by GitHub itself.
The two contexts are the ones ci.yml ACTUALLY reports on a push to main — measured, not read out
of the workflow. `strict` is false: it means `up to date with the base branch`, which a ref moved
by direct push has no use for. This cannot break a legitimate promotion: promote-release.mjs
already refuses a sha whose `ci` run is absent, unfinished or red, so every sha GitHub would
reject here is one the gate refuses anyway. The two agree rather than overlap.
WHAT IS STILL NOT CLOSED, said plainly rather than left to be discovered: someone with push
rights can open a pull request, let ci go green on its head sha, never merge it, and push THAT
sha here. So the residual exposure is content that PASSED CI BUT WAS NEVER REVIEWED OR MERGED —
narrower than arbitrary content, and not nothing. Closing it needs a repository RULESET on
refs/heads/release whose only bypass actor is the GitHub Actions app; `restrictions` here is
organisation-only and this is a personal repository, so this file cannot express it.
NO REVIEWS, on purpose: the promotion is a direct push, and a pull-request requirement would
break it outright. `lock_branch` stays false for the same reason — it would lock out the
workflow too.
